qs.q: What is the primary underlying nature of the brain disturbance in cerebral palsy?
o: A nonprogressive disturbance in the developing brain
qs.e: Cerebral palsy is attributed to nonprogressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain causing permanent movement and posture disorders. It is distinct from progressive neurodegenerative diseases.

qs.q: What proportion of children with cerebral palsy are estimated to have intrapartum asphyxia as an identifiable cause?
qs.e: Fewer than 10% of children with cerebral palsy have evidence of intrapartum asphyxia, as most cases stem from antenatal factors. Intrapartum factors are not the leading primary cause in most cohorts.

qs.q: Which maternal condition is strongly associated with a significant increase in the risk of cerebral palsy in normal birthweight infants?
o: Gestational diabetes mellitus in the mother
qs.e: Intrauterine exposure to maternal infection, such as chorioamnionitis and urinary tract infections, is associated with a significant increase in the risk of cerebral palsy. Gestational diabetes is not highlighted as a primary infectious risk factor for CP.

qs.q: Which specific brain lesion is a major contributor to cerebral palsy in premature infants and reflects vulnerability of immature oligodendroglia?
qs.e: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) reflects the vulnerability of immature oligodendroglia in premature infants to oxidative stress and ischemia. It remains a major lesion contributing to CP in preterm infants.

qs.q: How does the incidence of cerebral palsy in twin pregnancies compare to singleton pregnancies?
qs.e: Studies document a rate of cerebral palsy in twins that is 5 to 8 times greater than in singleton pregnancies. Triplets carry an even higher risk.

qs.q: An infant presents with decreased spontaneous movements on the affected side, early hand preference, and an arm more involved than the leg. Which motor syndrome of cerebral palsy is most likely?
qs.e: Infants with spastic hemiplegia have decreased spontaneous movements on the affected side and often show greater upper extremity involvement than lower extremity involvement. This presentation contrasts with symmetrical diplegia.

qs.q: Which diagnostic imaging modality is far more sensitive than a cranial CT scan for detecting most brain lesions seen with cerebral palsy?
qs.e: MRI is far more sensitive than cranial CT scan for most lesions seen with cerebral palsy, though CT may still be useful for calcifications associated with congenital infections. Ultrasound is also less detailed than MRI for parenchymal white matter changes.

qs.q: Which inherited thrombophilic disorder or factor is noted as a potential cause of focal cerebral infarction leading to hemiplegic cerebral palsy?
qs.e: Inherited clotting disorders such as the factor V Leiden mutation and the presence of anticardiolipin antibodies contribute to focal cerebral infarction and hemiplegic CP. The other options are hematologic conditions not primarily linked to stroke-related CP.

faq.a: The underlying brain injury is non‑progressive, but secondary problems such as contractures and scoliosis can worsen over time.
Many cases are linked to preventable perinatal events—adequate obstetric care, infection control, and neonatal resuscitation reduce risk.
MRI provides better detail of white‑matter injury and basal‑ganglia lesions, which are important for prognosis.
faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over CT?

exam: What bedside findings would help you differentiate spastic diplegia from spastic hemiplegia? — Look for bilateral lower‑limb stiffness with preserved upper‑limb tone (diplegia) versus unilateral tone increase and contralateral weakness (hemiplegia).

A 3‑year‑old with CP presents with fever, cough and new infiltrate on chest X‑ray. What is your immediate management? — Assume aspiration pneumonia; start empiric antibiotics covering anaerobes, assess airway protection, and arrange physiotherapy for chest clearance.
How does the GMFCS influence long‑term planning? — It predicts mobility, need for assistive devices, and risk of secondary complications, guiding therapy intensity and surgical referral.

Why is baclofen preferred over high‑dose diazepam for chronic spasticity? — Baclofen acts on spinal GABA‑B receptors with fewer sedative effects; diazepam can cause respiratory depression, especially in children with compromised airway.

A child with CP has worsening scoliosis. Which investigation is essential and why? — Full‑spine standing X‑ray; quantifies curve magnitude (Cobb angle) to decide on bracing versus surgical correction.

What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent neuro‑imaging in a child previously diagnosed with CP? — New focal neurological deficit or seizure change suggesting a superimposed lesion such as tumour or hydrocephalus.

Explain why routine metabolic screening is still performed in a child with established CP. — To exclude treatable metabolic disorders that can mimic or aggravate CP, especially when the clinical picture changes.

When is gastrostomy feeding indicated in CP and what are the benefits? — When chronic aspiration or poor oral intake persists despite therapy; it reduces pneumonia risk, improves nutrition, and supports growth.
ai.title: Cerebral Palsy
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a permanent disorder of movement and posture caused by non‑progressive injury to the developing brain. Severity is graded by motor function scales, and management focuses on preventing complications and optimizing function.

b: Non‑progressive brain injury
Motor impairment present before age 2
Abnormal tone (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic)
sections.p: CP describes a group of permanent motor disorders arising from injury to the fetal or infant brain before 2 years of age. Diagnosis is clinical, based on motor impairment, abnormal tone, and a history of perinatal or early‑life brain insult.

t.b: Confirms onset before 2 y and identifies risk factors; helps differentiate CP from progressive neurometabolic disease
Classifies functional level; guides prognosis and therapy planning

b: GMFCS Level I‑II: ambulant
GMFCS Level III‑V: limited or no ambulation
sections.p: The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) is the accepted tool, ranging from Level I (walks without limitation) to Level V (requires wheelchair and extensive assistance).

b: Perinatal hypoxic‑ischemic injury
Preterm birth with intraventricular haemorrhage
Neonatal sepsis (e.g., meningitis, malaria)
Maternal infections (HIV, syphilis, malaria)
Birth‑related trauma (shoulder dystocia, forceps)
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the common aetiologies are perinatal asphyxia, severe prematurity, neonatal infections, and birth‑trauma. Tropical infections and maternal conditions also contribute.

b: Spastic diplegia – leg‑dominant stiffness, common after birth asphyxia
Spastic hemiplegia – unilateral involvement, often from perinatal stroke
Dyskinetic (choreo‑athetoid) – fluctuating movements, basal ganglia injury
Associated problems: reflux, aspiration, contractures, scoliosis
sections.p: Children present with abnormal tone (spasticity, dystonia, ataxia), delayed motor milestones, and often associated feeding difficulties, seizures, or visual/hearing impairment.
Investigations aim to identify a treatable cause, assess brain injury, and detect complications. In low‑resource hospitals, many imaging modalities may be unavailable.

t.b: Detects intraventricular haemorrhage or cystic lesions; if unavailable, proceed with clinical staging
Defines pattern of injury (periventricular leukomalacia, basal ganglia lesions); guides prognosis
Excludes metabolic derangements that can mimic CP; normal results support non‑progressive diagnosis
Identifies infectious aetiologies common in East Africa; positive results prompt specific therapy

b: Recurrent aspiration pneumonia
Severe contractures limiting respiration
Scoliosis causing restrictive lung disease
Seizure clusters
Pressure ulcers
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent attention.

b: Physiotherapy and stretching to maintain range of motion
Oral motor therapy and positioning for safe feeding
Antispasticity agents (baclofen, diazepam) – avoid high‑dose benzodiazepines in severe hepatic disease
Botulinum toxin for focal spasticity when available
Surgical tendon release or selective dorsal rhizotomy for severe contractures
Nutritional support (NG tube or gastrostomy) for chronic aspiration risk
sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: treat any identifiable cause, optimise motor function, and prevent complications.

b: Quarterly motor assessment using GMFCS
Annual vision and hearing screening
Vaccination and infection prophylaxis (e.g., pneumococcal vaccine)
Parent education on positioning and skin care
sections.p: Regular review by a paediatric neurologist, physiotherapist, and nutritionist is essential. Early intervention programmes reduce long‑term disability.

b: Genetic neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., spinal muscular atrophy)
Metabolic encephalopathies (e.g., mitochondrial disease)
Acquired brain injury after age 2 (e.g., traumatic brain injury)
sections.p: Conditions that mimic CP must be excluded, especially those that are progressive.

b: Normal cranial ultrasound after 6 months does not rule out periventricular leukomalacia
Serum lactate may be normal in early mitochondrial disease
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite significant injury.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathing or cough suggesting aspiration pneumonia
New onset seizures or status epilepticus
Rapid development of contractures causing skin breakdown
